title: Lakshmana's rage and restraint
hook: the loyal younger brother says out loud what everyone else is only thinking

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's argument, won. Rama said, I didn't know your mind; come with me. Today we step back into Kausalya's room, where someone has been burning.

We've watched Rama be calm for days. It would be easy to think everyone in the palace felt as he did. Valmiki makes sure we don't. When Rama told his mother the news, Lakshmana stood silent in the room. Then, while Kausalya wept, he spoke, and out came the question the story has been holding back. This is wrong. Somebody should stop it. Why isn't anybody stopping it?
screen: `NOT EVERYONE IS CALM.` → `LAKSHMANA, SILENT IN THE ROOM.` → `WHY ISN'T ANYBODY STOPPING IT?`

segments.voice: Valmiki lets us hear every layer of Lakshmana's anger. First, fairness. Rama has done nothing wrong; who in the whole kingdom can name a single fault in him? To throw him out for no reason is against dharma itself. Second, the king. Lakshmana says what no one else will: the old man has been ruled by his desire for a young wife, and isn't fit to judge. He goes further still, with words against his own father that Valmiki records and we won't repeat here. Third, action. I'm armed, he tells Rama. I'm with you. If anyone in this city takes Bharata's side, I'll fight them all. Let Kausalya see it; let the whole world see it. It's frightening, and it's loyal: every word comes from love for his brother. Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for that devotion, and today it looks like a drawn bow. Kausalya, desperate, seizes on it. Listen to your brother, she tells Rama. Don't go. This is a harder test of Rama's calm than Kaikeyi was. Not from his opponent, but from someone on his side, offering exactly what part of him might want. The rage is real, it's righteous, and it's within reach. Tomorrow, Lakshmana's argument at its strongest, and what Rama does with it.
screen: `RAMA HAS DONE NOTHING WRONG.` · `THE OLD KING ISN'T FIT TO JUDGE.` · `I'M ARMED. I'M WITH YOU.` · `RAMA'S CALM, TESTED BY A FRIEND.` · then, large: `THE RAGE IS REAL, AND IT'S LOYAL.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you were angry on someone else's behalf, at an injustice done to a friend or family member, and let a little of that heat come back. Notice where it lives in the body: chest, hands, face. On each breath out, notice the love underneath it, the care that made you angry in the first place.
Lakshmana, Rama's loyal younger brother. Loyal to the bone, he says Rama has done no wrong and offers to fight the whole city for him.
Your line: I'm armed, I'm with you. Every word of Lakshmana's rage comes from love. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for a brother's devotion; this outburst in Kausalya's room shows that devotion as anger, before it learns restraint.

original.note: Sanskrit lakṣmaṇa: the name of Rama's younger brother, Sumitra's son, who stands beside him through the exile.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lakshmana just follows Rama quietly.
what it means: he erupts in rage at the injustice, out of love.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki lets a loyal hero speak harshly even of his own father and king, and leaves the words in the text rather than smoothing them away.

chat.says: Was Lakshmana angry at Rama for agreeing to go?
options: No, his anger was for Rama, at the injustice, and he offered to fight for him.
Yes, he was jealous that Rama had been chosen as heir instead of him.
No, he was angry at Kausalya for not stopping the king much sooner.
chat.meaning: Lakshmana's rage comes from love for Rama. He calls the exile unjust and offers to fight the whole city for him.
